section.heading: 6.6 Machine Learning and Linear Models
Machine Learning
section.paragraph: Machine learning uses linear models in situations where the machine is being trained to predict the outcome (dependent variables) based on the values of the inputs (independent variables). The machine is given a set of training data where the values of the independent and dependent variables are known. The machine then learns the relationship between the independent variables and the dependent variables. One type of learning is to fit a curve, such as a least-squares line or parabola, to the data. Once the machine has learned the pattern from the training data, it can then estimate the value of the output based on a given value for the input.
section.heading: Least-Squares Lines
section.paragraph: A common task in science and engineering is to analyze and understand relationships among several quantities that vary. This section describes a variety of situations in which data are used to build or verify a formula that predicts the value of one variable as a function of other variables. In each case, the problem will amount to solving a least-squares problem.

For easy application of the discussion to real problems that you may encounter later in your career, we choose notation that is commonly used in the statistical analysis of scientific and engineering data. Instead of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ , we write $$X\textit{\textbf{\beta }} = \mathbf{y}$$ and refer to $$X$$ as the design matrix, $$\textit{\textbf{\beta }}$$ as the parameter vector, and $$\textbf{y}$$ as the observation vector.

The simplest relation between two variables $$x$$ and $$y$$ is the linear equation $$y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x$$ .1 Experimental data often produce points $$\left( x_{1},y_{1} \right)$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\left( x_{n},y_{n} \right)$$ that, when graphed, seem to lie close to a line. We want to determine the parameters $$\beta_{0}$$ and $$\beta_{1}$$ that make the line as “close” to the points as possible.

Suppose $$\beta_{0}$$ and $$\beta_{1}$$ are fixed, and consider the line $$y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x$$ in Figure 1. Corresponding to each data point $$\left( x_{j} \text{,} y_{j} \right)$$ there is a point $$\left( x_{j} \text{,} \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x_{j} \right)$$ on the line with the same $$x \text{-coordinate}$$ . We call $$y_{j}$$ the observed value of $$y$$ and $$\beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x_{j}$$ the predicted $$y \text{-value}$$ (determined by the line). The difference between an observed $$y \text{-value}$$ and a predicted $$y \text{-value}$$ is called a residual.

image.alt: A graph shows a straight line labeled y equals beta subscript 0 baseline plus beta subscript 1 baseline x on a coordinate plane.

figure.caption: Figure 1 Fitting a line to experimental data

section.paragraph: There are several ways to measure how “close” the line is to the data. The usual choice (primarily because the mathematical calculations are simple) is to add the squares of the residuals. The least-squares line is the line $$y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x$$ that minimizes the sum of the squares of the residuals. This line is also called a line of regression of $$\mathbf{y}$$ on $$\mathbf{x}$$ , because any errors in the data are assumed to be only in the $$y \text{-coordinates}$$ . The coefficients $$\beta_{0}$$ , $$\beta_{1}$$ of the line are called (linear) regression coefficients.2
If the data points were on the line, the parameters $$\beta_{0}$$ and $$\beta_{1}$$ would satisfy the equations

image.alt: A table provides the predicted and observed y-values.

section.paragraph: We can write this system as

$$X \mathbf{\mathit{\beta}} = \textbf{y} , \text{where} X = \left[\right. 1 & x_{1} 1 & x_{2} \vdots & \vdots 1 & x_{n} \left]\right. , \mathbf{\mathit{\beta}} = \left[\right. \beta_{0} \beta_{1} \left]\right. , \textbf{y} = \left[\right. y_{1} y_{2} \vdots y_{n} \left]\right.$$

Of course, if the data points don’t lie on a line, then there are no parameters $$\beta_{0}$$ , $$\beta_{1}$$ for which the predicted $$y \text{-values}$$ in $$X\mathbf{\beta}$$ equal the observed $$y \text{-values}$$ in $$\textbf{y}$$ , and $$X\mathbf{\beta} = \textbf{y}$$ has no solution. This is a least-squares problem, $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ , with different notation!

The square of the distance between the vectors $$X\mathbf{\beta}$$ and $$\textbf{y}$$ is precisely the sum of the squares of the residuals. The $$\mathbf{\beta}$$ that minimizes this sum also minimizes the distance between $$X\mathbf{\beta}$$ and $$\textbf{y}$$ . Computing the least-squares solution of $$X \mathbf{\mathit{\beta}} = \textbf{y}$$ is equivalent to finding the $$\mathbf{\mathit{\beta}}$$ that determines the least-squares line in Figure 1.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Find the equation $$y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x$$ of the least-squares line that best fits the data points $$\left( 2,1 \right)$$ , $$(5,2)$$ , $$(7,3)$$ , and $$(8,3)$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Use the $$x \text{-coordinates}$$ of the data to build the design matrix $$X$$ in (1) and the $$y \text{-coordinates}$$ to build the observation vector $$\textbf{y}$$ :
$$X = \left[\right. 1 & 2 1 & 5 1 & 7 1 & 8 \left]\right. , \textbf{y} = \left[\right. 1 2 3 3 \left]\right.$$
For the least-squares solution of $$X\mathbf{\beta} = \textbf{y}$$ , obtain the normal equations (with the new notation):
$$X^{T} X \mathbf{\mathit{\beta}} = X^{T} \textbf{y}$$
That is, compute

$$X^{T} X & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 5 & 7 & 8\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 5 \\ 1 & 7 \\ 1 & 8\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}4 & 22 \\ 22 & 142\end{matrix} \left]\right. X^{T} \textbf{y} & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 5 & 7 & 8\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}9 \\ 57\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$
The normal equations are
$$\left[\right. 4 & 22 22 & 142 \left]\right. \left[\right. \beta_{0} \beta_{1} \left]\right. = \left[\right. 9 57 \left]\right.$$
Hence

$$\left[\right. \beta_{0} \beta_{1} \left]\right. = \left(\left[\right. 4 & 22 22 & 142 \left]\right.\right)^{- 1} \left[\right. 9 57 \left]\right. = \frac{1}{84} \left[\right. 142 & - 22 - 22 & 4 \left]\right. \left[\right. 9 57 \left]\right. = \frac{1}{84} \left[\right. 24 30 \left]\right. = \left[\right. 2 / 7 5 / 14 \left]\right.$$
Thus the least-squares line has the equation

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: If a machine learns the data from Example 1 by creating a least-squares line, what outcome will it predict for the inputs $$4$$ and $$6$$ ?
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The machine would perform the same calculations as in Example 1 to arrive at the least-squares line
as a reasonable pattern to use to predict the outcomes.
For the value $$x = 4$$ , the machine will predict an output of $$y = \frac{2}{7} + \frac{5}{14}(4) = \frac{12}{7}$$ .
For the value $$x = 6$$ , the machine will predict an output of $$y = \frac{2}{7} + \frac{5}{14}(6) = \frac{17}{7}$$ . See Figure 3.

image.alt: A graph shows machine-learned output along with the predicted point, learned line, and learning data points.

section.paragraph: A common practice before computing a least-squares line is to compute the average $$\overline{x}$$ of the original $$x \text{-values}$$ and form a new variable $$x^{\ast} = x - \overline{x}$$ . The new $$x \text{-data}$$ are said to be in mean-deviation form. In this case, the two columns of the design matrix will be orthogonal. Solution of the normal equations is simplified, just as in Example 4 in Section 6.5. See Exercises 23 and 24.
section.heading: The General Linear Model
section.paragraph: In some applications, it is necessary to fit data points with something other than a straight line. In the examples that follow, the matrix equation is still $$X\mathbf{\beta} = \textbf{y}$$ , but the specific form of $$X$$ changes from one problem to the next. Statisticians usually introduce a residual vector $$\mathbf{\mathit{\epsilon}}$$ , defined by $$\mathbf{\epsilon} = \mathbf{y} - X\mathbf{\beta}$$ , and write
$$\textbf{y} = X \mathbf{\mathit{\beta}} + \mathbf{\mathit{\epsilon}}$$

Any equation of this form is referred to as a linear model. Once $$X$$ and $$\textbf{y}$$ are determined, the goal is to minimize the length of $$\mathbf{\epsilon}$$ , which amounts to finding a least-squares solution of $$X\mathbf{\beta} = \textbf{y}$$ . In each case, the least-squares solution $$\widehat{\mathbf{\beta}}$$ is a solution of the normal equations
$$X^{T} X \mathbf{\mathit{\beta}} = X^{T} \textbf{y}$$
section.heading: Least-Squares Fitting of Other Curves
section.paragraph: When data points $$\left( x_{1} \text{,} y_{1} \right)$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\left( x_{n} \text{,} y_{n} \right)$$ on a scatter plot do not lie close to any line, it may be appropriate to postulate some other functional relationship between $$x$$ and $$y$$ .
The next two examples show how to fit data by curves that have the general form
$$y = \beta_{0} f_{0} \left(\right. x \left.\right) + \beta_{1} f_{1} \left(\right. x \left.\right) + \hdots + \beta_{k} f_{k} \left(\right. x \left.\right)$$

where $$f_{0}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$f_{k}$$ are known functions and $$\beta_{0}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\beta_{k}$$ are parameters that must be determined. As we will see, equation (2) describes a linear model because it is linear in the unknown parameters.

For a particular value of $$x$$ , (2) gives a predicted, or “fitted,” value of $$y$$ . The difference between the observed value and the predicted value is the residual. The parameters $$\beta_{0}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\beta_{k}$$ must be determined so as to minimize the sum of the squares of the residuals.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Suppose data points $$\left( x_{1},y_{1} \right)$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\left( x_{n},y_{n} \right)$$ appear to lie along some sort of parabola instead of a straight line. For instance, if the $$x \text{-coordinate}$$ denotes the production level for a company, and $$y$$ denotes the average cost per unit of operating at a level of $$x$$ units per day, then a typical average cost curve looks like a parabola that opens upward (Figure 4). In ecology, a parabolic curve that opens downward is used to model the net primary production of nutrients in a plant, as a function of the surface area of the foliage (Figure 5). It is a simple matter to write this system of equations in the form $$\mathbf{y} = X\mathbf{\beta} + \mathbf{\epsilon}$$ . To find $$X$$ , inspect the first few rows of the system and look for the pattern.

section.heading: Multiple Regression
section.paragraph: Suppose an experiment involves two independent variables—say, $$u$$ and $$v$$ —and one dependent variable, $$y$$ . A simple equation for predicting $$y$$ from $$u$$ and $$v$$ has the form
$$y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} u + \beta_{2} v$$
A more general prediction equation might have the form
This equation is used in geology, for instance, to model erosion surfaces, glacial cirques, soil pH, and other quantities. In such cases, the least-squares fit is called a trend surface.

Equations (4) and (5) both lead to a linear model because they are linear in the unknown parameters (even though $$u$$ and $$v$$ are multiplied). In general, a linear model will arise whenever $$y$$ is to be predicted by an equation of the form
$$y = \beta_{0} f_{0} \left(\right. u , v \left.\right) + \beta_{1} f_{1} \left(\right. u , v \left.\right) + \hdots + \beta_{k} f_{k} \left(\right. u , v \left.\right)$$
with $$f_{0}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$f_{k}$$ any sort of known functions and $$\beta_{0}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\beta_{k}$$ unknown weights.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: In geography, local models of terrain are constructed from data $$\left( u_{1},v_{1},y_{1} \right)$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\left( u_{n},v_{n},y_{n} \right)$$ , where $$u_{j}$$ , $$v_{j}$$ , and $$y_{j}$$ are latitude, longitude, and altitude, respectively. Describe the linear model based on (4) that gives a least-squares fit to such data. The solution is called the least-squares plane. See Figure 7.

image.alt: A figure shows a least squares plane placed horizontally. Ten points are seen above the plane connected by solid lines. Ten points are seen below the plane connected by dashed lines.

example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: We expect the data to satisfy the following equations:

$$y_{1} & = & \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} u_{1} + \beta_{2} v_{1} + \epsilon_{1} y_{2} & = & \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} u_{2} + \beta_{2} v_{2} + \epsilon_{2} \vdots & & \vdots y_{n} & = & \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} u_{n} + \beta_{2} v_{n} + \epsilon_{n}$$
This system has the matrix form $$\mathbf{y} = X\mathbf{\beta} + \mathbf{\epsilon}$$ , where

$$\begin{matrix} & & \text{Observation} & & & \text{Design} & & & \text{Parameter} & & & \text{Residual} \\ & & \text{vector} & & & \text{matrix} & & & \text{vector} & & & \text{vector} \\ \textbf{y} & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}y_{1} \\ y_{2} \\ \vdots \\ y_{n}\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & X & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & u_{1} & v_{1} \\ 1 & u_{2} & v_{2} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & u_{n} & v_{n}\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \mathbf{\mathit{\beta}} & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\beta_{0} \\ \beta_{1} \\ \beta_{2}\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \mathbf{\mathit{\epsilon}} & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\epsilon_{1} \\ \epsilon_{2} \\ \vdots \\ \epsilon_{n}\end{matrix} \left]\right.\end{matrix}$$

section.paragraph: Example 5 shows that the linear model for multiple regression has the same abstract form as the model for the simple regression in the earlier examples. Linear algebra gives us the power to understand the general principle behind all the linear models. Once $$X$$ is defined properly, the normal equations for $$\mathbf{\beta}$$ have the same matrix form, no matter how many variables are involved. Thus, for any linear model where $$X^{T} X$$ is invertible, the least-squares $$\widehat{\mathbf{\beta}}$$ is given by $$\left( X^{T} X)^{- 1}X^{T}\textbf{y} \right.$$ .

The term $$\beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x$$ gives the basic sales trend, and the sine term reflects the seasonal changes in sales. Give the design matrix and the parameter vector for the linear model that leads to a least-squares fit of the equation above. Assume the data are $$\left( x_{1},y_{1} \right)$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\left( x_{n},y_{n} \right)$$ .

section.paragraph: 1 This notation is commonly used for least-squares lines instead of $$y = mx + b$$ .

2 If the measurement errors are in $$x$$ instead of $$y$$ , simply interchange the coordinates of the data $$\left( x_{j},y_{j} \right)$$ before plotting the points and computing the regression line. If both coordinates are subject to possible error, then you might choose the line that minimizes the sum of the squares of the orthogonal (perpendicular) distances from the points to the line.

3 The basic idea of least-squares fitting of data is due to K. F. Gauss (and, independently, to A. Legendre), whose initial rise to fame occurred in 1801 when he used the method to determine the path of the asteroid Ceres. Forty days after the asteroid was discovered, it disappeared behind the sun. Gauss predicted it would appear ten months later and gave its location. The accuracy of the prediction astonished the European scientific community.
